title: Grade XI Physics – Unit 3: Full-Length 80-MCQ Summative Section A Practice
sourceDocument: NBF Grade XI Physics, Unit 3 textbook pp.33–52; FBISE Physics HSSC-I Assessment Framework and 50% MCQ Model Question Paper
sourceSection: 56 independent straight MCQs + 24 scenario MCQs in 6 complete 4-question stimuli; 6 adapted source exercise/numerical items, 74 original SLO practice questions
limitations: This is a full-length Section A count (80×0.5=40 practice marks) for Unit 3 only, NOT an official full-syllabus FBISE exam, official marking scheme, or fully verified assessment. Source-identified practice material remains provisional pending teacher academic QC. Formative B-03/B-11 excluded. Stage1 original file remains unchanged.

questions.stem: Which description best represents projectile motion after launch, in the absence of air resistance?

options.text: An object moving entirely independently of gravity
Only an object projected exactly vertically upward
An object moving under gravity after being projected into the air
Only horizontal motion without any gravitational force

questions.explanation: After launch, gravity acts on the projectile; the horizontal and vertical components of motion evolve independently.

questions.stem: At which location is the magnitude of an ideal projectile's vertical velocity component the smallest?

options.text: At landing at the launch height
At one-quarter of the flight time

questions.explanation: At the top, vᵧ = 0, the minimum possible magnitude.

questions.stem: After an ideal projectile has been released, the only force acting on it (neglecting air resistance) is:

questions.stem: For a fixed launch speed onto level ground, and no air resistance, the maximum projectile range is obtained at:
questions.explanation: R = (u²/g)sin(2θ), maximized when sin(2θ)=1, so θ = 45°.

questions.stem: During forward flight through still air, the horizontal velocity component of a projectile experiencing air resistance generally:

questions.stem: While a projectile is ascending, the vertical component of air resistance normally acts:

questions.stem: Two ideal projectiles at complementary launch angles have equal range at fixed speed and equal heights. With air resistance this equality:

questions.stem: In an ideal isolated elastic collision, which two total physical quantities are conserved?

options.text: Momentum and speed of each body
Kinetic energy and the velocity of each body
Momentum and the direction of motion of each body

questions.stem: If total kinetic energy before an isolated elastic collision is 80 J, the total kinetic energy afterward is:
questions.explanation: Total kinetic energy is conserved in an isolated elastic collision, so it remains 80 J.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct for an isolated system during an inelastic collision?

options.text: Both momentum and kinetic energy must always increase
Total momentum is destroyed when deformation occurs
Each object's momentum remains individually unchanged
Total momentum is conserved even though total kinetic energy may decrease

questions.explanation: The isolated system conserves total momentum, but some kinetic energy can transform into heat, sound or deformation.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: In an inelastic collision, part of the initial kinetic energy may be transferred into:

options.text: An increase in the system's external impulse

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy can change form in an inelastic collision; this does not violate overall energy conservation.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Two approaching objects stick together in an isolated collision. Compared with an elastic collision having the same initial conditions, the total kinetic energy after this collision is:

options.text: Unchanged because total momentum is conserved
Lower because some kinetic energy is converted into other forms
Greater because the bodies share a common velocity
Always zero regardless of the initial velocities

questions.explanation: In a non-trivial perfectly inelastic collision, momentum remains conserved, but some initial kinetic energy converts to heat, sound or deformation. An otherwise identical elastic collision conserves kinetic energy.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: A 4 kg body moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 2 kg body and they stick together. What is the decrease in total kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Momentum: (4)(3) + (2)(0) = 12 kg·m/s, so common speed = 12/6 = 2 m/s. K before = ½(4)(3²) = 18 J; K after = ½(6)(2²) = 12 J. Kinetic energy decreases by 6 J, while momentum remains conserved.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: Which conclusion best explains a decrease in total kinetic energy after an isolated collision?

options.text: Some kinetic energy has changed form, although total momentum is conserved
Total momentum must decrease by the same percentage
The law of conservation of energy has been violated
The mass of both objects must become zero

questions.explanation: Some mechanical kinetic energy converts into other forms; total momentum remains conserved in an isolated interaction.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23, FBISE HSSC-I Grade XI Assessment Framework; source-grounded but provisional educational practice

questions.stem: A train travelling at 24 m/s slows uniformly at 4 m/s². The time it takes to stop is:

questions.stem: A particle has initial velocity −6 m/s and constant acceleration +3 m/s² for 4 s. The total distance it travels is:
questions.explanation: It stops momentarily at t = 2 s after moving 6 m in the negative direction, then travels 6 m forward in the remaining 2 s. Total distance = 12 m; net displacement = 0.

questions.stem: An object is released from rest. Neglect air resistance and take g = 9.8 m/s². Its downward speed after 2 s is:
questions.explanation: For free fall from rest, v = gt = (9.8)(2) = 19.6 m/s downward.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 29.4 m/s. With g = 9.8 m/s² and no air drag, the time to reach its highest point is:
questions.explanation: At the top v = 0: 0 = 29.4 − 9.8t, so t = 3.0 s.

questions.stem: A vehicle's velocity increases uniformly from 12 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s. Its displacement during this interval is:
questions.explanation: With constant acceleration, s = (u+v)t/2 = (12+20)(4)/2 = 64 m.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: An object is launched horizontally from a cliff 45 m high. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, the time to reach level ground is:
questions.explanation: Vertical initial velocity is zero. From h = ½gt², t = √(2h/g) = √(90/10) = 3.0 s.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: A projectile is launched horizontally at 15 m/s. If its flight lasts 3 s without air resistance, its horizontal range is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal speed is constant: R = vₓt = (15)(3) = 45 m.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 45° above level ground and lands at the same height. With g = 10 m/s², its range is:
questions.explanation: R = u²sin(2θ)/g = 20²sin90°/10 = 40 m.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: A projectile is fired at 20 m/s and 30° above horizontal. Assuming no drag and g = 10 m/s², its maximum height above the launch point is:
questions.explanation: Initial vertical speed uᵧ = 20sin30° = 10 m/s; H = uᵧ²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5 m.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: At the highest point of an ideal projectile's flight, which statement is correct?

options.text: Both components of its velocity become zero
Its vertical velocity is zero while its horizontal velocity remains constant
Its downward gravitational acceleration becomes zero
Its horizontal acceleration suddenly becomes positive

questions.explanation: At the top vᵧ = 0, but vₓ = u cosθ is constant and gravity continues acting downward.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 30 m/s and 60° above horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, its horizontal velocity throughout flight is:
questions.explanation: vₓ = u cos60° = 30(0.5) = 15 m/s at every point.

questions.stem: Two projectiles launched from level ground at the same speed, at 25° and 65°, have equal ideal horizontal ranges because:

options.text: The angles add to 90° and sin(50°) = sin(130°)
Both have exactly the same maximum height
Both have exactly the same flight time
Gravity becomes zero at the highest points

questions.stem: In NBF Unit 3 Numerical 3.4, an ideal projectile is launched at 21.8 m/s at 35° and lands at its launch height. With g = 9.8 m/s², its flight time is approximately:
questions.explanation: T = 2u sinθ/g = 2(21.8)sin35°/9.8 ≈ 2.55 s, matching NBF exercise Numerical 3.4.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: While a projectile is moving upward through still air, its vertical acceleration (upward taken positive) has a magnitude that is:

options.text: Greater than g because both gravity and the vertical drag component point downward
Less than g because upward drag balances gravity
Always equal to g regardless of air resistance

questions.explanation: On ascent, the vertical components of both gravity and drag are downward, so the magnitude of downward vertical acceleration exceeds g while the projectile has an upward velocity component.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: The instantaneous direction of aerodynamic drag on a projectile moving through still air is generally:

options.text: Always directly downward irrespective of motion

questions.explanation: Resistive drag opposes the projectile's velocity relative to the air.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: Using the ideal no-air-resistance range equation for an otherwise identical flight affected by appreciable drag would generally:

options.text: Predict the exact range regardless of drag
Underestimate the range in every case
Make the calculated range independent of launch speed

questions.explanation: Ideal R = u²sin2θ/g assumes no resistive force; drag generally shortens an otherwise identical flight.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: During a projectile's forward motion through still air, the horizontal component of air drag gives an acceleration that points:

options.text: In the same forward direction as motion
In the same direction as the projectile's weight

questions.explanation: The horizontal component of resistive force opposes horizontal motion, so aₓ is backward while the projectile moves forward.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: Two 2 kg bodies collide elastically head-on. The first moves right at 4 m/s; the second is initially at rest. The first body's final velocity is:
questions.explanation: Equal masses exchange velocities in an ideal one-dimensional elastic collision: the first comes to rest.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: A 1-D elastic collision occurs with initial velocities u₁ = +8 m/s and u₂ = −2 m/s. The relative speed of separation after the collision is:
questions.explanation: Approach speed u₁−u₂ = 8−(−2)=10 m/s; for an elastic collision the separation speed is also 10 m/s.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: A 1 kg body moving right at 4 m/s elastically strikes a stationary 3 kg body head-on. The 1 kg body's final velocity is:
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: An isolated system has total kinetic energy 75 J before an ideal elastic collision. The system's total kinetic energy after the collision is:
questions.explanation: An ideal elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy of the isolated system, so K after = 75 J.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: Two identical masses approach head-on. Before an elastic collision the first has velocity +6 m/s and the second −2 m/s. Afterward, the first body's velocity is:
questions.explanation: In an ideal head-on elastic collision of equal masses, their signed velocities are exchanged. Thus v₁ = −2 m/s.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: A 2 kg object moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg object and the pair sticks together. The decrease in total kinetic energy is:
questions.explanation: Momentum gives shared v = (2×4)/(2+2)=2 m/s. Before K=½(2)(4²)=16 J; after K=½(4)(2²)=8 J, so the loss is 8 J.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: An isolated inelastic collision changes the system's kinetic energy from 72 J before impact to 48 J afterward. The fraction of initial kinetic energy transferred into other forms is:
questions.explanation: Decrease ΔK = 72−48 = 24 J, so fraction transferred = 24/72 = 1/3. Total energy is conserved in different forms.
questions.sloAlignment: NCP 2022–23 FBISE HSSC-I summative; teacher and science-review pending, original educational practice

questions.stem: In an isolated head-on collision, total momentum is conserved but the total kinetic energy becomes smaller afterward. The collision is:

options.text: Necessarily a collision in which both bodies stop

questions.explanation: An inelastic collision conserves isolated-system momentum but does not conserve kinetic energy; part of it changes into other forms.

questions.stimulusText: A ball rolls horizontally off a cliff 80 m above level ground with a horizontal speed of 15 m/s. Neglect air resistance and use g = 10 m/s². Take the horizontal direction positive and vertical displacement measured downward from the cliff top.

questions.stem: Their common final velocity is:
questions.explanation: Momentum before = 3(6)+1(−2)=16 kg·m/s; total mass =4 kg. Shared final v =16/4=+4 m/s.
